presentingComplaint: Generalized weakness, palpitations, and cramping for 3 days
history: 58-year-old woman with hypertension on long-term furosemide and a recent 5-day illness with profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting presents with progressive generalized weakness, muscle cramps, and palpitations. She reports poor oral intake during the diarrhoeal illness and has continued her usual diuretic dose. No chest pain. No prior arrhythmia history. No laxative abuse. No diuretic other than furosemide; denies licorice ingestion.
examination: Alert, mildly fatigued-appearing woman. Generalized muscle weakness (proximal > distal), diminished deep tendon reflexes. No focal neurological deficit. Mild diffuse abdominal discomfort, no distension. Chvostek and Trousseau signs negative. No oedema.
imaging: ECG: prolonged QU interval, prominent U waves, flattened T waves, occasional PVCs
microbiology: Stool studies not sent (self-limited pre-admission diarrhoeal illness); no active infective workup indicated at presentation
differentialDiagnoses: GI-loss (diarrhoea/vomiting) plus loop-diuretic-induced hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
Diuretic-induced metabolic alkalosis with secondary hypokalaemia
finalDiagnosis: Combined hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia due to GI losses (diarrhoea/vomiting) compounded by chronic loop diuretic use, with arrhythmia risk
citations: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guidelines (electrolyte disorder management principles)
contraindications: Avoid rapid/undiluted IV potassium bolus (arrhythmogenic) — must be given as controlled infusion with cardiac monitoring
Potassium repletion alone will fail if hypomagnesaemia is not corrected concurrently (renal K wasting persists via ROMK channel effect until Mg is replete)
Avoid additional loop diuretic dosing until electrolytes corrected; reassess diuretic necessity
Caution with concurrent QT-prolonging drugs given ECG changes
edgeCases: Hypokalaemia refractory to potassium replacement should always prompt magnesium measurement and repletion
Low urine chloride (<25 mmol/L) here favours GI loss/contraction alkalosis over primary renal tubular wasting (Bartter/Gitelman, which typically show higher urine chloride)
Concurrent metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 31, pH 7.49) is expected from both vomiting/diarrhoea-associated volume contraction and chronic loop diuretic use
